title: The Crow and the Serpent

full_text:
In the branches of an ancient banyan tree, a mother crow had built her nest, hatching four gentle fledglings. But in the hollow of the tree’s roots dwelt a venomous black cobra, which crawled up the trunk each spring and devoured the young birds, leaving the parent crows in agonizing grief.

The crow flew to her wise friend, the jackal, weeping: 'I cannot bear this sorrow! I must fly into the cobra’s hole and peck out his eyes, even if his fangs slay me!'

The jackal shook his head: 'Do not throw yourself upon venom with brute force, sister! A direct attack is suicide, but subtle wit can enlist the strength of giants to destroy your enemy.'

The jackal instructed the crow in a clever plan.

The crow flew to the royal garden of the Sultan’s palace, where the princess was bathing in an outdoor marble pool, having placed her diamond necklace upon a velvet cushion on the terrace.

The crow swept down with a rush of wings, snatched the glittering necklace in her beak, and flew slowly above the garden, just within sight of the royal guards!

The guards shouted: 'The crow has stolen the princess’s necklace!' and pursued the bird with spears and cudgels.

The crow flew directly to the banyan tree, hovered above the roots, and dropped the diamond necklace into the dark hollow where the cobra slept.

The guards rushed to the roots, saw the glittering diamonds, and when the furious cobra emerged with flared hood to strike, the guards dispatched the serpent with their staves, recovered the princess’s necklace, and returned to the palace.

The mother crow nested in peace, thanking the jackal, having learned that intellect can defeat venom without receiving a single wound.
moral: Brain outmatches venom; subtle strategy uses the power of the mighty to remove dangerous adversaries.
